_categoryVocabulary.note: PROPOSED. No English entry in the platform DB has a category field, so there is nothing to match against and this is a decision rather than a lookup. Derived by grouping the 44 live English entries; the grouping covers all 44 with no residue, which is the only evidence I have that the vocabulary fits. values.Retrieval & Location: the child is looking in the wrong place, or at the wrong thing in the right place
values.Inference & Reasoning: the child has the text and draws the wrong conclusion from it
values.Vocabulary in Context: the child takes the wrong meaning for a word the passage fixes
values.Writer's Technique: the child cannot say what the writer is doing, or mistakes whose voice is speaking
values.Option Behaviour: the child's answer is produced by the option set rather than by the passage

_meta._axisVocabulary: Mirrors maths: TOPIC where the error is about the reading skill, PROCESS where it is about how the child behaves under test conditions. All seven here are TOPIC.
_meta._distractorClassVocabulary: Mirrors maths: 'derivable' where the distractor can be produced mechanically from the text — take the wrong element, the other conjunct, the commonest sense, the look-alike word — and 'conceptual' where it cannot. Six of the seven are derivable. en-whole-text-absence-asserted is conceptual, because no line produces it: it is generated by failing to notice a pattern held across the whole text.

misconceptions.description: The option states something that is true inside the cited window and answers a different question from the one asked. The child has located the right lines and taken the wrong element out of them. A named sub-route is the WRONG SPEAKER: the material is inside the window but belongs to the other party in an exchange — one child's answer offered where the other child's instruction was asked for. The cure is the same, so the sub-route shares the hint.
misconceptions.childHint: This one is in the lines. Check it answers the question you were asked.
misconceptions.boundaries: Against en-wrong-scope-retrieval the test is LOCATION: outside the stem's named window is wrong-scope, inside it is this. Against en-plausible-not-stated the test is TRUTH: those options are absent from the passage, these are present in it. Against en-inference-literal-lookalike the test is WHAT THE OPTION IS MADE OF: literal-lookalike reuses the wording of the window as its answer; these are usually reworded and are wrong because of the relation they stand in to the question. Against en-attribute-transfer and en-agent-patient-reversal the test is WHETHER A RELATION IS SCRAMBLED: two things swapping properties or roles is transfer or reversal; one true thing offered in place of another true thing, with no swap, is this. Against en-coordination-wrong-conjunct the test is WHETHER A CONNECTIVE DID THE WORK: if the option is true of the other half of a named coordination, it is that entry.
misconceptions.hintDirection: back to the question that was asked
misconceptions.categoryNote: WITHDRAWN, and null rather than guessed. I proposed a fresh six-value vocabulary because I searched every artefact I hold and found no English entry carrying a category. misconceptions.importPriority: R67. directionTest.rule: No hint may send the child where a sibling already sends her.
directionTest.direction: back to the question that was asked
directionTest.result: PASS — no other entry sends the child here.
directionTest.limit: catches IDENTICAL directions, not CONVERGENT ones. The rejected dominant-sense draft would have passed a strict-equality test while doing the erosion it was rejected for. Blunt case mechanical, near-miss human.

coachedKeyTest.rule: A hint blocks the error the entry names; it does not coach the key.
coachedKeyTest.result: BLOCKS: the child has verified the option IS in the passage and stopped there; the hint sends her to the question she was actually asked. Does not coach the key.
coachedKeyTest.why: Not mechanisable. A blocking and a coaching hint can be identical in every measurable property; the difference is which way the instruction runs relative to the error, and the error lives in the description rather than in the hint. A proxy would pass things it should not, and a passing proxy is believed.

misconceptions.description: The passage carries an explicit negative — no, not, never, nothing, without, could not, sha'n't — and the option states the affirmative. The child has read the content words of the sentence and dropped the word that reverses them. Requires a negative WORD in a named line; a negation sustained across a whole text with no such word is en-whole-text-absence-asserted.
misconceptions.childHint: Find the small negative word in the line before you decide. One 'not' changes the whole answer.
misconceptions.boundaries: Against en-relation-word-flipped the test is WHAT THE DROPPED WORD DOES: a relation word joins two propositions and flipping it rearranges how they relate; a negative operates on one proposition and dropping it inverts that proposition's truth. Against en-extreme-option-pull the test is DIRECTION: that entry ADDS an absolute the text does not carry, this one REMOVES one it does. Against en-plausible-not-stated the test is whether the passage addresses the point at all: here it addresses it and says no. Against en-minimal-pair-skim the test is WHOSE PROPERTY IT IS: that is a property of the option set, this is a property of one option against the passage. Against en-whole-text-absence-asserted the test is WHETHER A NEGATIVE WORD EXISTS TO DROP.

misconceptions.description: The child applies the word's commonest everyday sense in a context that does not support it. The sense chosen is a real sense of the same word; it is simply the one that arrives first, and the sentence around the word is what should have displaced it. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items: it occurs wherever a word's sense is load-bearing, including on technique stems.
misconceptions.boundaries: Against en-vocab-neighbouring-sense the test is WHICH SENSE ARRIVES FIRST for an eleven-year-old: the commonest is this, any other real sense is neighbouring. That boundary is a judgement about children rather than about text and is the softest line in this set. Against en-vocab-form-lookalike the test is WHETHER THE MEANING BELONGS TO THIS WORD AT ALL: here it does.
misconceptions._supersededHint: You know one meaning for this word. Read the words either side of it and check that meaning still works there.
misconceptions.hintRuling: Anne's wording, taken verbatim, replacing my drafted 'Read the words either side of it and check that meaning still works there.' Her ground, recorded with the entry because it governs every hint in this family: the drafted version is en-vocab-neighbouring-sense's instruction in different words, and it is wrong for THIS child. The neighbouring-sense child has several meanings live and needs the local words to adjudicate between them. The dominant-sense child has ONE meaning and does not know there is a competition — sending her to adjacent words sends her to check something she has no reason to doubt. She needs to test her one meaning against what the sentence is doing. The structural reason: this keeps the three hints pointing in three directions — one meaning tested against sense, several meanings adjudicated by neighbours, wrong word caught by spelling. Two of them saying 'look nearby' erodes the split.

misconceptions.hintNote:
CHILD HINT IS NULL AND STAYS NULL UNTIL THE STORED FIELD CAN BE QUOTED. Anne's ruling, R25 at the one entry whose failure mode is her name on words she did not write: a confirmation obtained from a transcription tests nothing. If my typing is faithful she learns nothing; if it is unfaithful she confirms the error. Sending her my retyping and asking 'is this what you wrote?' is the en-narrator-voice-as-fact round exactly — a reported opinion presented in flat certain sentences and then taken as the thing itself.

So the value I had here has been WITHDRAWN rather than re-sent. It is preserved in _transcribedHintWithdrawn purely so the eventual diff has something to diff against, and it must NOT be the source for the import.

PROTOCOL. The hint enters this row by being read from a stored field in an artefact Anne wrote or the platform holds — never retyped from a message. compare_stored_hint.py does the comparison character for character and reports the first differing offset, so the check is mechanical rather than eyeballed. Until that artefact exists this entry cannot go into any batch, and the validator enforces it.

misconceptions.description: The target word sits in a coordination — X and Y, X as well as Y, X as Y, X beside Y — and the child attaches the meaning to the wrong conjunct. She takes the half of the pair she read last, or the half that is easier to picture, and glosses the target with it. The error is syntactic: she has parsed which item the word attaches to incorrectly, and the option she picks is usually TRUE of the other conjunct, which is why it survives a check against the passage.
misconceptions.childHint: This word is joined to another by 'and' or 'as well as'. Joined means they are two different things, not one.
misconceptions.boundaries: Against en-within-span-wrong-element, from which this was separated, the test is WHETHER A CONNECTIVE DID THE WORK: if the option is true of the other half of a named coordination — and, as, as well as, beside — it is this; any other true-but-irrelevant element of the window is the parent. The cure differs and that is the ground for the split: the parent's cure is semantic (does this answer the question asked?), this one's is syntactic (which half of the 'and' does the word belong to?), and one hint cannot serve both. Against en-attribute-transfer the test is WHETHER TWO THINGS SWAP: transfer moves a property from one entity to another; this attaches the target word to the wrong entity without moving anything.

rejectedFirstDraft.whyKept: Anne's instruction: keep it in the record. It shows erosion happening in the direction hardest to see — narrowing a parent's instruction FEELS like sharpening rather than duplicating. misconceptions.description: The passage sustains an ABSENCE across its whole length — it never states a feeling, never names a motive, never gives a verdict — and the option asserts the withheld thing as though it were there. There is no negative word to drop, because the negation is a property of the text rather than of any line: the child has failed to notice something maintained across sixty lines, not misread a word in one. Characteristically the option is defeated by no single line and only by the absence itself, so its disposal must cite the SPAN of the withholding rather than a disposal point.
misconceptions.childHint: Before you say the writer told you this, look right through and find where. If it is said nowhere, he never told you.
misconceptions.boundaries: Against en-negation-dropped, from which this was separated, the test is WHETHER A NEGATIVE WORD EXISTS TO DROP: if you can quote no, not, never, without or sha'n't in a named line, it is that entry; if the negation is carried by the text refusing to say something, it is this. That entry's hint — find the small negative word in the line — is actively wrong here, because no such word exists to find. Against en-plausible-not-stated the test is WHETHER THE WITHHOLDING IS THE DEVICE: plausible-not-stated covers anything the passage happens not to mention; this covers something the passage is deliberately and repeatedly not saying, which is what whole-text T4 items are built on.

misconceptions.draftingWarning: COACHING RECURS HERE, AND HERE MORE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE. Anne's note, recorded on the entry for whoever drafts the next whole-text hint: a whole-text T4 key is a RELATION, and the error is usually asserting half of it or the wrong half. So advice about the relation helps BOTH children — the one who has to see the relation to answer correctly, and the one who asserted half of it. The error and the key sit closer together on this construction than anywhere else in the library, which is why my first draft coached the key while passing the direction test, and why the coached-key question has to be asked deliberately on any hint written for a whole-text entry rather than assumed from the direction being distinct.
misconceptions.hintRuling: Anne's ground: it opens on the assertion she is about to make and makes her discharge it, rather than pointing at the absence and letting her reach the key by a route the item is supposed to test. The closing sentence does the work — it states plainly the thing this child does not believe.

rejectedFirstDraft.whyKept: Coached the key while PASSING the direction check — it pointed where no sibling pointed. The only worked example in the library of a hint failing Q7 and clearing Q1's mechanical sibling.
